The vote row uses $d{=}1$; depth does not change the answer under the frozen budget (Section~\ref{sec:method}).

\paragraph{How the evaluators fail.} On the test split, the 70B predictor rejected every root candidate in 70 of 390 searches, which then return the proposer's first candidate (7 correct, 57 inapplicable, 6 not closer); the search has no re-proposal step, and these searches explain most of 70B's lower call count (11.4).
On the validation split, three failure modes stood out. The 0--10 scores of the 8B model collapse
onto a few values (most often 2), so they rarely separate siblings. The comparative vote of the 8B
model is strongly position-biased: it chose the first option in only 3 of 39 votes, although the
proposer lists its best candidate first, which drove its accuracy to $0.05$; the 70B model showed no
such bias. Finally, asking the predictor to flag inapplicable actions is precise but rarely used by
8B, while 70B flags more of them but also rejects applicable ones.

Table~\ref{tab:domains} breaks the frozen search's accuracy down by domain. 8B solves no Alfred or Gripper question, and the largest gains from scale are on Swap, Satellite and Depots.

\paragraph{Re-created validation comparison.} The evaluator comparison behind the frozen design (23 Oct) was not kept, so we re-created it on 22 Nov with the final code, pre-registered in \texttt{experiments/preregistration\_22nov.md} (Table~\ref{tab:validation-search}). Fixed scoring (13.0 of 40 on average) is slightly ahead of the frozen 0--10 evaluator (12.3), so the frozen evaluator is not the best here; both are ahead of steps (10.0), random scores (8.7) and vote (4.7, at $d{=}1$, about 5 calls per question). The choice was within noise, and fixed scoring also leads on test. Seed 1 of the 0--10, steps and vote runs replayed every call from the cache, so those three runs repeat calls made in the original validation runs.
